A \\emph{survivor} is a correct program whose algorithm is not banned. Finally, we ran an evaluator-guided island-model search in the manner of FunSearch~\\citep{RomeraParedes2023}, in which the model mutates programs and a fixed evaluator keeps the best ones across generations. Every correct program labelled outside its task's catalogue was compared with a corpus of known solutions (about 18,000 programs built from LeetCode, textbook and benchmark solutions), read by blind LLM judges gated on known controls, and read manually. Zero novel programs in $n$ correct ones is reported with the rule-of-three bound $3/n$.\n\n\\section{Experimental Setup}\n\\label{sec:setup}\n\n\\paragraph{Pre-registration.} Every decisive prediction, threshold and analysis rule was written to a SHA-256 hash chain before the samples it governs were drawn, and each artifact's chain verifies end to end. The same seed experiment pre-registered four predictions: a temperature change count of at most 1 of 20 seeds in each of four cells (three tasks without thinking, shortest path with thinking); phrasings per idea that grow with temperature; a random push that changes at least 5 of 20 seeds on shortest path and on $k$-th smallest; and a positive per-seed contrast between push and temperature, pooled over those two tasks, at one-sided $p < 0.05$, which was the experiment's single entry in the secondary test family. The experiment is confirmed only if all four hold. The composed law's criterion was an MAE of at most 0.10 with $H(A \\mid \\text{class})$ at most 0.3 bits per unit, and passing on at least 70\\% of scored units including at least 3 held-out units, with at least 4 held-out units scored.\n\n\\paragraph{Units and samples.} The temperature block used 20 seeds per task and condition for Qwen3-8B on grid, shortest path and $k$-th smallest, run in an FP8 engine whose rows reproduced the same cells of an earlier run token for token (200 of 200). The composed law was developed on trapped rain water, valid anagram and minimum spanning tree weight in Qwen3-8B and tested, before any Qwen3-8B sweep sample, on held-out units from two other families: substring search and first and last position in gemma-3-4b-it, and the grid task in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Each unit was swept on 100 fresh shared streams at $T$ = 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3 under top-$p$ 1 and top-$k$ 10, in bfloat16. Escapes under activation pushes are not an artefact of the 8-bit engine: the same push directions that changed the algorithm in FP8 change it in bfloat16 (26 of 40 directions on connected components against 29 in FP8, and 6 against 8 on shortest path).\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-6/experiment-29}}\n\n\\paragraph{Statistics.} Paired binary contrasts use the exact McNemar test~\\citep{Mcnemar1947}, the per-seed contrast between push and temperature a sign-flip test with a slot bootstrap interval, and proportions Wilson or Clopper-Pearson intervals. Every headline number was re-derived from raw rows by an independent script sharing no code with the analysis, and placebo versions of each test (shuffled conditions, shuffled temperature labels, shuffled token maps) were run and rejected at about their nominal rate. Code, prompts, raw generations, labels and the hash chains of every experiment are released with the paper, and each result below links to the code that produced it.\n\n\\section{Results}\n\\label{sec:results}\n\n\\subsection{A task-state push changes the algorithm where temperature does not}\n\\label{sec:res-push}\n\nOn the same random streams, a random task-state push changed Qwen3-8B's algorithm in more seeds than temperature did, by a paired difference of 0.545 per seed (95\\% bootstrap CI 0.41 to 0.67), pooled over shortest path and $k$-th smallest (40 seeds; Figure~\\ref{fig:headline} and Table~\\ref{tab:seed}). For each seed, the contrast is the push's change indicator, averaged over the 20 three-direction subsets (each a union over three directions at $\\alpha = 1$ and $T = 1.0$), minus the seed's change indicator across the four temperatures. It was pre-registered as the experiment's single entry in the secondary test family and held, with a one-sided sign-flip $p$ of $1.0\\times10^{-5}$. A within-seed permutation of conditions never reaches the observed mean (maximum placebo mean 0.155 in 200 permutations). The experiment as a whole is graded partial: its pre-registered prediction that the push changes at least 5 of 20 seeds held on shortest path (17.25) but failed on $k$-th smallest (4.55). The contrast was run only in the 8-bit (FP8 W8A8) engine and was not rerun in bfloat16. The push itself does reproduce in bfloat16 at the same absolute dose unit (Section~\\ref{sec:setup}).\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\caption{Seeds (of 20) whose algorithm changes across the conditions of a block, Qwen3-8B, same random stream per seed, 8-bit W8A8 engine except the thinking-mode arm (vLLM). Push rows are the mean over the 20 three-direction subsets of six fixed directions of the number of seeds whose label differs anywhere among the unpushed arm and the three directions.}\n  \\label{tab:seed}\n  \\small\n  \\begin{tabularx}{\\linewidth}{@{}L C{2.5cm} C{2.5cm} C{2.2cm}@{}}\n    \\toprule\n    Conditions on the same seeds & Shortest path (Dijkstra) & $k$-th smallest (full sort) & Grid path (BFS) \\\\\n    \\midrule\n    Temperature 0.3, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3, top-$p$ 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\\n    The same, plus top-$k$ 10 at $T$ 0.7 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\\n    The same, plus min-$p$ 0.1 at $T$ 2.0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\\\\n    Temperature 0.3 to 1.3, thinking mode & 0 & not run & 0 (of 10) \\\\\n    \\midrule\n    Random task-state push, $\\alpha = 1$, $T$ 1.0 & 17.25 & 4.55 & 2.50 \\\\\n    Random task-state push, $\\alpha = 2$, $T$ 1.0 & 19.05 & 10.60 & 8.70 \\\\\n    \\bottomrule\n  \\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nA single push direction at $\\alpha = 1$ changed 7, 10, 15, 17, 3 and 8 of 20 seeds on shortest path and up to 7 of 20 on $k$-th smallest. The algorithms the changed programs moved to, their \\emph{landings}, were Bellman-Ford/SPFA (52 of 60 off-default programs on shortest path) and quickselect (11 of 11 on $k$-th smallest). The push is not free: pass rates on shortest path fell from 1.00 to 0.63 at $\\alpha = 1$ and 0.42 at $\\alpha = 2$.\n\nTemperature, on the same seeds, never changed the algorithm on any of the three default tasks. Across $T$ = 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3, all 20 seeds kept their algorithm on shortest path (Dijkstra), on $k$-th smallest (full sort) and on the grid task (BFS). The change count is 0 of 20 per task, with an exact 95\\% upper bound of 0.168 on the per-seed change rate. This was a separate pre-registered prediction (at most 1 of 20 seeds per cell), and it held under every reading: counting only correct programs, counting invalid outputs as a label, and adding top-$k$ 10 as a fifth condition all leave the count at 0. Adding min-$p$ 0.1 at $T = 2.0$ changes one seed on shortest path and one on $k$-th smallest. With thinking mode enabled, shortest path kept Dijkstra in 20 of 20 seeds, every final program and every first approach named in the reasoning was Dijkstra, and all 100 traces completed within the 16k-token cap. The reduced grid arm kept BFS in 10 of 10 seeds.\n\nPhrasings, in contrast, grow with temperature (Figure~\\ref{fig:phrasings}). On the grid task the number of phrasing clusters among 20 programs rose from 3 at $T = 0.3$ to 10, 12 and 13 at $T$ = 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3, while the number of distinct algorithms stayed at 1 on all three tasks at every temperature. The pooled slope of log phrasings per idea on temperature is 0.70 per unit $T$ (95\\% CI 0.35 to 0.93) at Jaccard threshold 0.8, and 0.64 [0.30, 0.89] and 0.81 [0.33, 0.98] at 0.7 and 0.9. Almost all of the growth comes from the grid task, while shortest path moves from 1 to 2 clusters and $k$-th smallest stays at 2.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig3_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Phrasing-cluster and distinct-algorithm counts across sampling temperature, under a shared random stream (Qwen3-8B, non-thinking mode, top-$p$ 1, 20 seeds per task, one program per seed and temperature; same seeds as Figure~\\ref{fig:headline} and Table~\\ref{tab:seed}). Solid lines with markers give phrasing clusters among the 20 same-seed programs on each task -- blue circles for grid path (BFS), orange squares for shortest path (Dijkstra), green triangles for $k$-th smallest (full sort) -- where a cluster is a connected component of programs whose identifier-normalised AST 4-gram Jaccard similarity is at least 0.8. The black dashed line with diamond markers gives distinct algorithms among the same programs, which is 1 on all three tasks at every temperature, as the in-figure annotation states (algorithm changed in 0 of 20 seeds per task; exact 95\\% upper bound 0.168 on the per-seed change rate). Phrasing diversity rises steeply with temperature on the grid-path task (3 to 13 clusters) and stays close to flat on the other two (1 rising to 2 on shortest path; constant at 2 on $k$-th smallest), while the dashed line never leaves 1.}\n  \\label{fig:phrasings}\n\\end{figure}\n\nThe temperature null replicates outside the seed-coupled design and the 8-bit engine. With 100 independent samples per cell, 797 of 800 grid programs were BFS and 797 of 800 shortest path programs were Dijkstra across eight temperature and sampler cells in non-thinking mode, and 800 of 800 in thinking mode. Over the same cells, grid phrasing clusters at threshold 0.8 rose from 4 to 36 with top-$k$ 10 and from 3 to 24 with top-$p$ 0.95. The literal setting of thinking mode with top-$k$ 10 under one seed per stream again changed the shortest path algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds (one-sided 95\\% upper bound 0.139),\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-5/experiment-27}} and in bfloat16, 100 samples at $T = 1.3$ from the forking position left the default unchanged on four tasks (Section~\\ref{sec:res-fork}). At tight temperature the model therefore writes one idea in a few phrasings, and loosening temperature multiplies the phrasings of that idea rather than adding ideas.\n\nWhich default a model writes depends on the model. Asked for a path search on a grid, Qwen3-8B writes BFS in 99 of 100 programs at $T = 1.0$ and Dijkstra in 100 of 100 on weighted shortest path. Gemma-3-4B writes DFS in 139 and BFS in 61 of 200 grid programs.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-6/experiment-31}} Llama-3.1-8B attempts BFS in 77 and DFS in 20 of 100, but its correct grid programs are all BFS.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-2/experiment-10}, \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-3/evaluation-2}}\n\n\\subsection{One or two forking tokens settle the algorithm}\n\\label{sec:res-fork}\n\nPrefix resampling places the decision at a single token after a shared opening on every unit where the instruct model writes two algorithms (Table~\\ref{tab:law}, fourth column). On minimum spanning tree weight the 61-token opening is followed by the word after the comment marker \\code{\\#}: \\tok{Kr} (probability 0.72) leads to Kruskal in every continuation, and \\tok{Prim} (0.27) to Prim in 97\\%. On trapped rain water, after \\code{if not height: return 0}, \\tok{n} leads to prefix and suffix arrays and \\tok{left} to two pointers. On valid anagram, after the length check, \\tok{return} leads to sorting and \\tok{count} to counting. Given the forking token's class, the remaining entropy of the algorithm is 0.050 bits [95\\% CI 0.014, 0.096], 0.153 and 0.189 bits on these three units, against the pre-registered limit of 0.3. A blind locator with a frozen change-point rule recovered the same tokens on fresh paths and reached at most 0.004 bits on the five Qwen3-8B and Gemma units. The same structure appears in other tasks and families. Connected components in Qwen3-8B is settled at generated tokens 10 to 11, where a \\tok{parent} or \\code{def find} line leads to union-find and \\code{def dfs} to graph search, with 0 bits left at token 11.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-7/experiment-34}} Gemma's grid prompt forks at response index 32: \\tok{visited} leads to DFS ($P(\\text{BFS}) = 0.011$), and a newline, \\code{if} or \\tok{queue} to BFS (0.95 to 1.00). Shortest path has no single forking token within its first 60 tokens.\n\nOn the default tasks the forking token is decided by a wide margin. The teacher-forced fork margin of the default is 7.46 nats on the grid task, 4.85 on shortest path, 17.04 on connected components and 6.10 on $k$-th smallest. Dividing these logits by 1.3 predicts at most 0.02 of samples off the default at $T = 1.3$, and 100 samples at $T = 1.3$ from the forking position produced no program off the default on any of the four tasks. A further 20 samples gave one off-default program each on the grid and shortest path tasks. The temperature null of Section~\\ref{sec:res-push} is what these margins predict: a temperature of 1.3 scales a 5 to 17 nat gap by $1/1.3$ and leaves the alternative out of reach.\n\n\\subsection{The forking-token logits predict the temperature response}\n\\label{sec:res-law}\n\nWhere the forking token is contested, the composed law predicts how temperature moves the algorithm mix (Table~\\ref{tab:law} and Figure~\\ref{fig:law}). The law was committed before any temperature sample and scored on 100 fresh shared streams per cell. It passed its unit criterion on five of six units: the three development units in Qwen3-8B (MAE 0.029, 0.054 and 0.043) and both held-out Gemma units (0.033 on substring search and 0.014 on first and last position). On first and last position the first forking token is impure, and the second level found inside it lowers the error from 0.051 for the single-fork law to 0.014 (bootstrap 95\\% CI of the difference $-0.051$ to $-0.011$). Lowering temperature from 1.0 to 0.3 removed the minority in one direction only on both Gemma units (10:0 and 13:0 discordant streams, McNemar $p = 0.001$ and $1.2\\times10^{-4}$) and on minimum spanning tree weight (18:0, $p = 3.8\\times10^{-6}$).\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\caption{The composed temperature law against its four rivals: mean absolute error (mean total variation distance over $T$ = 0.3, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3; 100 shared streams per cell). Development units were used to build the law; held-out units were committed and swept before any development-unit sweep. Lowest error per row in bold.}\n  \\label{tab:law}\n  \\footnotesize\n  \\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{2.6pt}\n  \\begin{tabularx}{\\linewidth}{@{}L C{0.75cm} R{1.55cm} R{1.45cm} C{1.05cm} C{0.85cm} C{1.1cm} C{0.95cm} C{1.3cm} C{1.25cm} C{0.6cm}@{}}\n    \\toprule\n    Unit (model) & Held out & Minority algorithm & Forking token(s) & Composed law & Flat & Tempering & Single fork & Highest-entropy position & $H(A \\mid \\text{class})$, bits & Pass \\\\\n    \\midrule\n    Trapped rain water (Qwen3-8B) & no & Two pointers & 18 and 19 & \\textbf{0.029} & 0.055 & 0.070 & 0.038 & 0.037 & $<0.001$ & yes \\\\\n    Valid anagram (Qwen3-8B) & no & Fixed count array & 24 and 26 & 0.054 & \\textbf{0.030} & 0.091 & 0.054 & 0.071 & $<0.001$ & yes \\\\\n    Minimum spanning tree weight (Qwen3-8B) & no & Prim & 61 & \\textbf{0.043} & 0.093 & 0.058 & \\textbf{0.043} & 0.045 & 0.004 & yes \\\\\n    Substring search (Gemma-3-4B) & yes & Built-in index & 31 & 0.033 & 0.043 & \\textbf{0.023} & 0.033 & 0.036 & 0.001 & yes \\\\\n    First and last position (Gemma-3-4B) & yes & Binary search & 12 and 24 & \\textbf{0.014} & 0.073 & 0.018 & 0.051 & 0.017 & 0.001 & yes \\\\\n    Grid path (Llama-3.1-8B) & yes & DFS & after a 52-token opening & 0.142 & 0.138 & 0.143 & 0.142 & \\textbf{0.134} & 0.63 & no \\\\\n    \\bottomrule\n  \\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nThe pre-registered claim is graded partial. Five of six scored units pass (0.83, above the 0.70 bar), but only three held-out units were scored where the claim required four, so the held-out criterion is underpowered rather than met. No held-out unit exceeded the disconfirming error of 0.2. The law is also not clearly better than simpler rivals. It has the lowest error on three of six units and beats the flat law on four of six (exact sign test $p = 0.34$). Slot-bootstrap intervals of the difference exclude 0 on minimum spanning tree weight [$-0.050$, $-0.025$], first and last position [$-0.081$, $-0.018$] and substring search [$-0.041$, $-0.002$]. Algorithm-level tempering beats it on substring search, and the flat law beats it on valid anagram, where temperature barely moves the mix. The law adds most where an impure first fork needs the second level and where the minority is not simply sharpened away.\n\nOn Llama-3.1-8B's grid task every predictor fails. Llama reaches the forking tokens through many openings, so the two confirmed openings cover about 2\\% of samples and the committed law is almost the flat law. At $T = 1.3$, 72 of 100 programs run to the token cap and the pass rate falls to 0.04, a collapse into unusable code that no algorithm-level law predicts. An earlier, smaller test of the single-fork law on 50 streams per cell passed on one of three Qwen3-8B units. Replaying each stream's own uniforms through the committed token classes reproduced the observed shares there (0.08, 0.18, 0.18 and 0.16 against 0.10, 0.18, 0.18 and 0.20 on trapped rain water), locating the misses in the finite sample rather than in the mechanism.\n\nApplying temperature only at the forking token tests the account causally. With the dose committed from teacher-forced logits, predicted algorithm shares matched the observed ones with MAE 0.010 to 0.047 on five located units, and correct-only Hill-1 on valid anagram rose from 1.78 to 2.78 at a cost of 2 percentage points of pass rate.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-8/experiment-39}} On collapsed connected components the same treatment reached DFS in only 3 and 9 of 50 programs, and the larger dose cost 14 percentage points of pass rate because the alternative tokens at the fork break the format.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig4_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Predicted and observed share of the minority algorithm at four sampling temperatures (0.3, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3; top-$p$ = 1, $N$ = 100 generations per cell, shared random streams across temperatures), for six algorithm-choice units: three Qwen3-8B development units -- (a) trapped rain water: two pointers, (b) valid anagram: fixed count array, (c) minimum spanning tree weight: Prim -- and three held-out units -- (d) Gemma-3-4B substring search: built-in index, (e) Gemma-3-4B first/last position: binary search, (f) Llama-3.1-8B grid path: DFS. Black circles give the observed minority share with vertical Wilson 95\\% confidence intervals; the solid blue line with small markers is the composed forking-token law's prediction, fixed before any temperature sample; the dashed grey line is a flat-law reference (the $T$ = 1 share held constant across temperature). Each panel title gives the mean absolute error, over the four temperature points, of the composed law and the flat law respectively. The composed law tracks the observed trend, rising or near-flat, on five of six panels, including both held-out Gemma-3-4B units (d, e); on the held-out Llama-3.1-8B grid-path unit (f) both the composed and flat lines stay nearly constant and neither tracks the non-monotonic observed points, consistent with that unit's pass rate falling from 0.22 to 0.04 between $T$ = 0.3 and $T$ = 1.3, where most generated programs become unusable.}\n  \\label{fig:law}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{What sets the forking token}\n\\label{sec:res-sets}\n\nThe task-specification states carry the choice into the forking token (Table~\\ref{tab:exchange}). Writing the task-specification states of a prompt that names the minority algorithm into its padding twin produced that algorithm in 30 of 30 shared streams on all three mixed units, with every program passing. The padding twin alone gave 0 to 7 of 30, and a random exchange of matched norm 0 to 12 of 30. The argmax at the forking token flips with it (\\tok{Kr} to \\tok{Prim}), and the fork margin moves by 4.87 to 22.12 nats toward the minority, against at most 2.00 nats for the random exchange. The same exchange carries a prohibition. We wrote the task-specification states of a shortest path prompt that bans Dijkstra, at all 36 blocks, into a token-length-matched neutral twin, the same prohibition sentence with irrelevant nouns in place of the algorithm. The twin then wrote correct Bellman-Ford/SPFA in 21 of 30 streams; a post hoc McNemar test against a matched random exchange gives 21:0 ($p = 9.5\\times10^{-7}$).\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-6/experiment-30}}\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\caption{Exchanging the task-specification states of a forced minority prompt into its padding twin (Qwen3-8B, bfloat16, 30 shared streams per arm). Shares are of attempted programs; the fork-margin change is in nats toward the minority.}\n  \\label{tab:exchange}\n  \\small\n  \\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{3.5pt}\n  \\begin{tabularx}{\\linewidth}{@{}L C{1.35cm} C{2.0cm} C{1.8cm} C{2.3cm} C{2.3cm}@{}}\n    \\toprule\n    Unit & Padding twin & Forced prompt's states exchanged in & Random exchange, matched norm & Exchange vs twin, discordant pairs ($p$) & Fork-margin change, exchange / random \\\\\n    \\midrule\n    Minimum spanning tree weight (Prim) & 0.23 & 1.00 & 0.40 & 23:0 ($1.2\\times10^{-7}$) & $-4.87$ / $-1.25$ \\\\\n    Trapped rain water (two pointers) & 0.13 & 1.00 & 0.13 & 26:0 ($1.5\\times10^{-8}$) & $-5.50$ / $-2.00$ \\\\\n    Valid anagram (fixed count array) & 0.00 & 1.00 & 0.00 & 30:0 ($9.3\\times10^{-10}$) & $-22.12$ / $+0.26$ \\\\\n    \\bottomrule\n  \\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nPost-training made the fork margins (Figure~\\ref{fig:base}). On identical chat-templated ids, Qwen3-8B's fork margin exceeds Qwen3-8B-Base's by 3.27 nats on the grid task, 13.41 on connected components and 2.11 on shortest path, the three default tasks, and by 1.84 and 1.53 nats on the two mixed units. Without chat tokens the gains on the default tasks are 5.31, 11.05 and 2.69 nats, so the template does not produce them. At 64 ordinary phrasing positions per program the two models differ little: the base model's next-token entropy is higher by 0.21 to 0.34 nats, and the instruct model's token is the base model's top token at 90.6\\% to 95.3\\% of phrasing positions on the default tasks. At the forking token, the instruct model's choice is the base model's second or third choice in 20, 17 and 19 of 20 programs. On the default tasks the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the two models is 7.3 to 12.0 times larger at the fork than at phrasing positions, but only 1.5 to 1.9 times larger than at phrasing positions matched for base-model entropy, which matches the known concentration of post-training shifts at high-entropy tokens~\\citep{Meng2026}. The instruct default is therefore not the base model's average answer: on minimum spanning tree weight the base model's fork distribution, pushed through the instruct model's continuations, would give Prim 0.68 where the instruct model writes Kruskal 0.78.\n\nReading the choice before the forking token was not possible with the readouts we tried, which fits a decision made at that token. A natural language autoencoder on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct~\\citep{Yang2024} named the planned algorithm at end-of-prompt positions in 0 of 112 cases, although at the algorithm-name token itself its explanations named the algorithm 80\\% to 89\\% of the time.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-6/experiment-32}} Sparse autoencoder features from Gemma Scope 2, the successor release of Gemma Scope~\\citep{Lieberum2024}, read Gemma's fork log-odds across 120 prompt variants ($R^2 = 0.66$ against 0.18 for a text baseline), but a ridge readout of the raw residual reached 0.72. Clamping features also steered the fork less than a difference-in-means direction ($+1.78$ against $+4.04$ nats at matched norm). Distributed alignment search at the forking token produced edits that moved the algorithm, but permuted-label and random-initialisation controls kept 0.63 to 0.87 and 0.69 of the effect, so no certified low-rank variable for the algorithm was found.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-8/experiment-40}} Path patching located a stack of MLPs and attention heads at the forking position that carries the fork logit, but at the committed dose five matched random components flipped nearly as many programs as the top five (7:1 discordant streams on minimum spanning tree weight, two-sided $p = 0.070$, and 0:1 on connected components).\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-8/experiment-41}} A logit-lens reading found no layer at which a ban vetoes the default at the token that first names the algorithm, because the choice is already made before it.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-2/experiment-8}} A community Jacobian lens failed its own gate against the logit lens on Qwen3-8B (top-1 agreement 0.104 against 0.291 at layer 27), so it was not used further.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-2/experiment-12}} Thought-anchor resampling of thinking traces~\\citep{Bogdan2025} under a BFS ban showed DFS fixed from the first resampling point in 4 of 4 traces.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig5_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Fork margin — the teacher-forced log-probability gap, in nats, between the token class leading to the instruct model's default algorithm and the best alternative class — for Qwen3-8B (instruct; dark blue bars) and Qwen3-8B-Base (grey bars) on identical chat-templated token ids, across five coding tasks. Bars show the mean over five prompt templates; whiskers span the minimum to the maximum over those templates. A dotted vertical line and italic headers separate the three default tasks (grid path/BFS, connected components/union-find, shortest path/Dijkstra) from the two mixed units (minimum spanning tree weight/Kruskal, trapped rain water/prefix-and-suffix maxima); the number above each pair is post-training's gain in mean fork margin, instruct minus base: +3.27, +13.41 and +2.11 nats on the default tasks, +1.84 and +1.53 nats on the mixed units. Over the same five templates and the same programs, the base model's next-token entropy at 64 ordinary (non-decision) phrasing positions per program was only 0.21-0.34 nats higher than the instruct model's, so post-training's effect on the output distribution is concentrated at the forking token rather than spread across the prompt.}\n  \\label{fig:base}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{Other controls reweight the same repertoire}\n\\label{sec:res-other}\n\nControls other than temperature moved programs among known algorithms when they moved them at all (Table~\\ref{tab:controls}). In Table~\\ref{tab:controls} a fixed push direction \\emph{escapes} when, over its first 10 samples, the share of attempts off the default exceeds that of the unpushed prompt by at least 0.20 at a pass rate of at least 0.8 times the unpushed prompt's, with a confirmation at 30 samples by an exact binomial test. Random context seeds left the default intact: with \\code{seed=d32qxk4nt43} or \\code{seed=(horse chair roof love)} prepended, the grid task stayed BFS in 100 of 100 programs and shortest path Dijkstra in 100 of 100, although the word seed moved the residual state at the last prompt token 1.555 times as far as switching between paraphrases of the prompt does. Instructions moved claims more than code. ``Make a fully novel algorithm never seen before'' lowered the Dijkstra share by 14.6 points, toward Bellman-Ford/SPFA. Under two 2,000-word novelty instructions, 84\\% of outputs claimed a new algorithm, 39\\% of those contained no code, and 75\\% of the rest were catalogue algorithms.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-3/experiment-18}} An audit of every correct program outside the catalogue from these early decoding conditions found none novel. grid: +2.2 points bidirectional BFS ($p = 0.078$) & 0 \\\\\n    ``Make a fully novel algorithm never seen before'' & Shortest path: Dijkstra share $-14.6$ points (to Bellman-Ford/SPFA); grid: $-3.7$ points & 0 \\\\\n    2,000-word novelty instructions (575 outputs) & 84\\% claim a new algorithm; 75\\% of claims with code are catalogue algorithms & 0 of 38 correct off-catalogue \\\\\n    Ban of the default by name & Lands on one substitute: grid DFS 257 of 257, shortest path Bellman-Ford/SPFA 255 of 260 & 0 \\\\\n    Ban of five grid algorithms by name (10 open configurations) & Only Qwen3-32B with thinking reaches 0.20 correct survivors (17/50 = 0.34 [0.22, 0.48]); others re-implement banned algorithms & 0 of 27 audited \\\\\n    Random task-state push (40 fixed directions, $\\alpha = 2$, bfloat16) & 26 of 40 directions escape on connected components and 6 of 40 on shortest path; landings DFS/BFS and Bellman-Ford/SPFA & 0 of 10,651 correct \\\\\n    Temperature at the forking token only & Valid anagram Hill-1 1.78 to 2.78 (pass rate $-2$ points); connected components DFS at most 9/50 & 0 of 5,543 correct \\\\\n    Evaluator-guided island-model search ($k$-th smallest, bin packing, TSP) & $k$-th smallest: 78 of 2,500 known techniques outside the catalogue vs 2 of 500 for the instruction alone; bin packing: beats best fit on held-out data & 0 confirmed \\\\\n    \\bottomrule\n  \\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nBans relocate the default within the repertoire. Whether a single ban is obeyed depends on its wording. On 12 bench tasks the template alone gives a likelihood ratio of 374 on 4 degrees of freedom for avoidance, and the wording ``X is not allowed here.'' fails on 10 of 12 tasks, in line with the sensitivity of models to prompt formatting~\\citep{Sclar2023}.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-3/experiment-13}} Where it is obeyed, a single ban of the default by name lands on one substitute, DFS for BFS and Bellman-Ford/SPFA for Dijkstra, recomputed over all pooled ban samples.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-3/experiment-16}} Banning five grid algorithms at once fails in most models. Across ten open configurations only Qwen3-32B with thinking clears the pre-registered bar of 0.20 correct survivors.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-8/experiment-44}} Qwen3-14B with thinking reaches 0.14 and Qwen3-32B without thinking 0.08, while Qwen3-8B with and without thinking, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-14B without thinking, gemma-3-27b-it, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct and gemma-3-4b-it reach 0.00; these models keep writing BFS or DFS, often without naming it. Lexical compliance, the share of programs that name no banned algorithm, exceeded mechanistic compliance, the share whose runtime behaviour is not a banned algorithm, by 0.70 pooled over ten configurations, a descriptive figure because the expansion-order tracer failed its gold gate.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-9/experiment-45}} With an exact behavioural instrument on online bin packing, Qwen3-8B without thinking obeyed a five-name ban by name in 0.91 of programs but by mechanism in 0.51 (difference 0.40 [0.21, 0.55]), while Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with thinking left the banned rules.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-10/experiment-54}}\n\nThe audits found no correct novel algorithm under any single-sample control, including 0 of 10,651 correct programs under random pushes and 0 of 4,703 in the temperature-law sweeps (rule-of-three bound 0.0006).\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-4/experiment-22}} Evaluator-guided search did better than the textbook rule without producing a confirmed new idea. Qwen3-32B with thinking writes BFS in 91 of 100 baseline programs; under the ban its six correct catalogue survivors are all unit-weight Dijkstra, and on held-out ban templates 9 of 9 are. On a map of the ten grid algorithms built from forced prompts that name them (block 31), unit-weight Dijkstra is the non-banned algorithm farthest from the banned five, with a geodesic distance, measured on a $k$-nearest-neighbour graph of the individual states with $k = 15$, of 1.63 times the median of the non-banned algorithms.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-9/experiment-46}} On a map built from name-scrubbed programs (block 33), it lies at the edge, at 0.67 times the median and nearest to greedy best-first search. Distances on the name-built map track the lexical overlap of the algorithm names (Spearman $-0.61$ at $k = 15$) and do not survive a within-algorithm alias test, so names and mechanisms are confounded there.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-9/evaluation-8}} The landing evidence is weak at the level of algorithms: the algorithm-level permutation $p$ is 0.20, its floor, and the opposite reading held in 10 of 15 robustness cells. The geometry is also correlational. Pushing Qwen3-8B's grid states inside the named map toward the survivor centroids produced BFS in 300 of 300 programs.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig6_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Activation-space maps of ten grid-search algorithms in Qwen3-32B (4-bit weights, thinking mode), with point coordinates from classical multidimensional scaling (MDS; arbitrary axis orientation, arbitrary units) of Euclidean distances between each algorithm's residual-stream centroid. Marker shape distinguishes the five algorithms named in the ban (cross: BFS, DFS, IDDFS, A*, greedy best-first) from the rest (circle). Marker fill colour, on the shared colour bar at right (``programs under the ban (of 50)'', light grey to dark red, 0-8), gives how many of 50 programs sampled under the five-name ban implemented that algorithm. A thick black ring marks unit-weight Dijkstra, the non-banned algorithm written most often under the ban (6/50); a thin ring marks BFS, the modal default with no ban in effect (91/100, noted beside it). (a) Map built from named prompts (block 31): centroids of 300 forced ``Implement $\\langle$algorithm$\\rangle$'' prompts (30 per algorithm, 10 algorithms), mean-pooled over the task-specification tokens; the top two MDS axes carry 50\\% and 17\\% of the variance. On a $k$=15 nearest-neighbour geodesic graph, unit-weight Dijkstra sits opposite the banned set (geodesic distance 1.63$\\times$ the median distance among non-banned algorithms). (b) Map built from name-scrubbed programs (block 33): centroids of name-scrubbed, hidden-test-verified programs for the six algorithms with at least 10 programs (20 each, 17 for IDA*; 117 programs total), mean-pooled over the generated code tokens; the top two axes carry 48\\% and 40\\% of the variance. The two maps disagree on whether the ban's main survivor lands opposite the banned algorithms or beside them; the geometry is correlational, not a steering result.}\n  \\label{fig:geometry}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\nThe headline contrast follows from where each control acts. The algorithm a code model writes behaves like a near-discrete decision taken at one or two tokens early in the program, and temperature acts on that decision only through the next-token distribution there; a push of the task-specification states acts upstream, on the states that set that distribution (Section~\\ref{sec:res-sets}). This single account explains the three regimes we observed. Where post-training has widened the fork margin to 4.85 to 17.04 nats, a temperature of 1.3 cannot reach the alternative, so the algorithm is fixed while every other position, where the next token is less certain, varies more. That is the phrasing growth of Figure~\\ref{fig:phrasings}. Where the forking token is contested, temperature sharpens or flattens the same two or three known algorithms at the rate the forking-token logits predict. And where the model reaches the decision through many openings, as Llama does on the grid task, the choice is spread over the opening and no single-token law captures it. In the terms of the question that motivates this work, a tight temperature with top-$k$ 10 gives one idea in a few phrasings, and a loose one gives the same idea, or the same few ideas, in more phrasings.\n\nThis account reconciles two findings that look contradictory. \\citet{Lee2025} report that temperature above 1 raises algorithmic diversity among correct programs, and we find that temperature never changes the algorithm on default tasks. Both hold. On tasks whose fork is contested, temperature moves mass between known algorithms at the predicted rate; Prim on minimum spanning tree weight rises from 0.07 at $T = 0.3$ to 0.31 at $T = 1.3$. On tasks whose fork is decided by several nats, it does not. A diversity evaluation that pools tasks will see an average of the two. Our results also bear on the claim that a model returns the average answer and that only context moves it elsewhere. The instruct default is not the base model's average: post-training moved and sharpened one token, often promoting the base model's second or third choice, and left the repertoire unchanged.\n\nFor practice, the account says where to spend randomness. Temperature is a poor exploration control for algorithm choice, and on contested units its effect can be predicted before sampling from the forking-token logits. Controls that act upstream of the fork, such as context that implies an algorithm, a list-then-pick prompt, or perturbations of the task-specification states, do change the algorithm, but they move it to the runner-up the model already knows, and at a cost in correctness. The audits found no route from any single-sample control to a correct novel algorithm. An evaluator that keeps improvements across generations made the same 8B model better than the textbook rule on bin packing, which is where the field's discovery systems operate~\\citep{RomeraParedes2023,Novikov2025}. Whether it made the model new remains open after the replication found none.\n\nFor interpretability, the results suggest that pre-code readouts of a plan should be validated against the forking token. Natural language and sparse-feature readouts found no verbalised plan before the code, and fitted subspace edits at the fork moved the algorithm without passing the controls that would make them a variable of the model, consistent with the interpretability illusions that subspace patching can produce~\\citep{Makelov2023}. The forking token is where intervention is cheap and measurable, but a certified mechanism for the choice is still missing.\n\n\\section{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\nThe headline contrast between the push and temperature ran only in an 8-bit (FP8 W8A8) engine and was not rerun in bfloat16; the push alone reproduces in bfloat16 at the same absolute dose unit, but the paired contrast was not repeated, and it pools two tasks, with the grid task moving only 2.50 of 20 seeds. Most results come from one model, Qwen3-8B, in non-thinking mode. The composed law was tested on three held-out units in two other families; two passed and Llama's grid task failed, below the four held-out units the pre-registered claim required, so the law's generality is an open question. The law was also not clearly better than a flat no-change baseline (four of six units, sign test $p = 0.34$), which means that much of its accuracy reflects how little temperature moves these units. The same-seed temperature null rests on 20 seeds per task, which bounds the per-seed change rate below 0.17 per task, not at zero, and it ran with 8-bit linear layers; the bfloat16 fork margins and the independent-sample grid agree with it, but the thinking-mode evidence is limited to shortest path and a 10-seed grid arm.\n\nThe tasks are short, well-known programming problems whose solutions are likely memorised, with catalogues of three to ten known algorithms; the conclusions may not hold for open-ended programs or for problems without a textbook solution. Experiments ran on different engines (bfloat16 and FP8 linear layers, vLLM and Hugging Face); push escapes reproduced in bfloat16, but pushed cells showed precision sensitivity at the level of single streams. Phrasing clusters depend on a Jaccard threshold over identifier-normalised AST shingles, and the growth was driven mostly by the grid task.\n\nLabels and the novelty audit carry their own uncertainty. Labellers were gated per task, but the gate failed by its strict criteria for the independent-sample decoding experiment and for the path-task runtime-against-AST agreement ($\\kappa = 0.753$), and the expansion-order tracer used for the five-name ban failed its gold gate, so those numbers are descriptive. In the evaluator-guided search no LLM judge passed its control gate, so novelty there rests on manual reads, and one reader's eight candidates were not reproduced by the replication. The activation-space geometry is correlational, and the name-built map is confounded by lexical overlap between algorithm names.\n\n\\section{Conclusion}\n\\label{sec:conclusion}\n\nOn the same random streams, a random push of Qwen3-8B's task-specification states changed the algorithm in more seeds than temperature did, by 0.545 per seed (95\\% CI 0.41 to 0.67) over shortest path and $k$-th smallest, a pre-registered contrast that held in an 8-bit engine and is untested in bfloat16. Temperature from 0.3 to 1.3 left the default algorithm unchanged in all 60 task-seeds while phrasings multiplied, because a forking token, not temperature, chooses the algorithm. Fork margins of 4.85 to 17.04 nats on the default tasks, widened by post-training, account for the null, and on contested forks the forking-token logits committed before sampling predicted the temperature response within 0.014 to 0.054 total variation on five of six units. No control we tested produced a correct algorithm outside the known repertoire.\n\nFuture work follows directly:\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item testing the composed law on more held-out units and families, including models that reach the fork through many openings;\n  \\item extending the forking-token analysis to reasoning traces, where the first approach named was fixed in every trace we read;\n  \\item spending sampling randomness at forking tokens inside evaluator-guided search, and measuring whether it buys ideas rather than phrasings;\n  \\item searching for a variable of the algorithm choice that passes label-permutation and random-initialisation controls.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\section*{Code and Data Availability}\n\nCode, prompts, raw generations, algorithm labels and the pre-registration hash chains of every experiment are public at \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract}; the footnotes in Sections~\\ref{sec:intro} to~\\ref{sec:results} link each result to the code that produced it.\n\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n\\bibliography{references}\n\n\\end{document}\n", "structuredPatch": [], "originalFile": null, "userModified": false}

r"""Sampling temperature is often treated as the creativity control of a language model. body = re.sub(r'\$[^$]*\$', 'X', body)
body = re.sub(r'\\(cite[pt]?|ref|label|section\*?|subsection|paragraph|emph|textbf|code|tok|texttt)\{([^}]*)\}', lambda m: m.group(2) if m.group(1) in ('emph','textbf','code','tok','texttt','section','section*','subsection','paragraph') else 'R', body)
body = re.sub(r'\\[a-zA-Z]+\*?', ' ', body); body = re.sub(r'[{}~]', ' ', body)
words = re.findall(r"[A-Za-z][A-Za-z'-]*|\d[\d.,]*", body); W = len(words)

banned = ['delve','underscore','showcase','intricate','pivotal','realm','commendable','meticulous','tapestry','garner','multifaceted','it is worth noting','plays a crucial role','not only']

sents = [s for s in re.split(r'(?<=[.!?])\s+(?=[A-Z])', re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', body)) if len(s.split()) > 2]
lens = sorted(len(s.split()) for s in sents); q = statistics.quantiles(lens, n=4)

#!/bin/bash
# Rebuild paper.pdf from paper.tex and references.bib with the full LaTeX sequence.
# BibTeX is called as `bibtex` when it is on PATH, else as `bibtex.original`
# (the name it has on the machine this paper was built on).

rm -f paper.aux paper.bbl paper.blg paper.out
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode paper.tex > /dev/null

pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode paper.tex > /dev/null
grep -n "^!" paper.log || echo "No LaTeX errors."
pdfinfo paper.pdf 2>/dev/null | grep Pages

# A Random Activation Push Changes a Code Model's Algorithm Where Temperature Does Not

LaTeX source, bibliography, figures and compiled PDF of the paper. The paper asks whether
sampling temperature changes *which algorithm* a code model implements, as opposed to how it
writes the same algorithm. It answers on shared random streams (common random numbers), with
every program labelled by its runtime behaviour on hidden tests.

**Headline finding.** On the same random streams, a random push of Qwen3-8B's residual-stream
states at the prompt's task-specification tokens changed the algorithm in more seeds than
temperature did, by a paired difference of 0.545 per seed (95% CI 0.41 to 0.67), pooled over
shortest path and k-th smallest (40 seeds). This pre-registered contrast held in a single
experiment whose overall pre-registered verdict is partial. It ran only in an 8-bit (FP8 W8A8)
engine and is untested in bfloat16. Temperature from 0.3 to 1.3 changed the algorithm in 0 of
20 seeds on each of three tasks while phrasings multiplied. One or two forking tokens settle the
algorithm, and the default leads there by 4.85 to 17.04 nats on the default tasks.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
|-|-|
| `paper.tex` | LaTeX source: generic `article` preamble (no target journal was named), 8 sections, 6 figures, 4 tables |
| `paper.pdf` | Compiled paper (25 pages including references) |
| `references.bib` | Bibliography, fetched from Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and Crossref, then checked against Crossref and arXiv records |
| `references.json` | Fetch record for every bibliography entry (source database, DOI or arXiv id, title, first author, year) |
| `paper.bbl` | BibTeX output, kept so the PDF can be rebuilt without re-running BibTeX |
| `paper.aux`, `paper.log`, `paper.blg`, `paper.out` | LaTeX build byproducts |
| `figures/fig1_v0.pdf` | Figure 1: same-seed algorithm changes, temperature against a task-state push (headline) |
| `figures/fig2_v0.jpg` | Figure 2: schematic of where the algorithm is decided (concept figure, not data) |
| `figures/fig3_v0.pdf` | Figure 3: phrasing clusters against distinct algorithms across temperature |
| `figures/fig4_v0.pdf` | Figure 4: composed forking-token law against observed minority shares, six units |
| `figures/fig5_v0.pdf` | Figure 5: fork margins of Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-8B-Base |
| `figures/fig6_v0.pdf` | Figure 6: activation-space maps of ten grid algorithms under a five-name ban |
| `figures/*_spec.json` | Plot specifications of the data figures (the numbers each figure draws) |
| `build.sh` | Rebuilds `paper.pdf` with the full pdflatex, bibtex, pdflatex, pdflatex sequence |

The experiments behind every result are in the public code repository that the paper's
footnotes link:
<https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract>.

## How to build

Requires a TeX Live installation with `pdflatex`, BibTeX, `natbib`, `tabularx`, `xurl`,
`microtype`, `caption` and the PostScript Times fonts (`mathptmx`, `helvet`, `courier`).

```bash
./build.sh
```

The script runs `pdflatex`, then `bibtex` (or `bibtex.original` where `bibtex` is not on PATH),
then `pdflatex` twice. After any change to `references.bib`, it deletes `paper.aux` and
`paper.bbl` first, so stale entries never print.

## Restoring removed files

No files were marked for deletion. Every file in this directory is source, text or a figure
under 2 MB, so `.aii/manifest.yaml` lists no entries and nothing needs restoring.

**Where `paper.tex` covers each part of the request:**
1. Behavioural analysis first: Sections 5.1 and 5.5, Tables 1 and 4, Figure 3.
2. Open-weight instruction-tuned models: Qwen3-8B, Gemma-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-14B/32B (Section 3.1).
3. Interpretability: natural language autoencoder, sparse autoencoder, distributed alignment search, path patching, logit lens and Jacobian lens in Section 5.4; geodesic distances and MDS in Section 5.6.
4. Is temperature the creativity knob, always with the same seed: Section 3.3, Section 5.1, Figure 1, Table 1.
